questions.question_text: A Wyoming buyer hires a licensee as their agent. Which duty does the agent owe?
distractors: Honesty and fair dealing only
Disclosure of material facts only
Accounting and confidentiality only
questions.explanation: Under W.S. §33-28-304(a), a licensee engaged by a buyer must perform the written agreement, exercise reasonable skill and care, and promote the buyer's interests with 'utmost good faith, loyalty and fidelity' — including presenting all offers timely, disclosing adverse material facts actually known, counseling on known material benefits and risks, and accounting timely for money and property. Wyoming reserves this level of duty for agency: §33-28-305(b)(ii)(K) requires an intermediary to disclose that an intermediary 'owes no fiduciary duty either to buyer or seller.' (Note: §33-28-301 was repealed in 2011; the agent duty lists are §33-28-303 for seller's agents and §33-28-304 for buyer's agents.)

questions.question_text: A seller contacts a brokerage but does not sign a listing agreement. What relationship exists?
distractors: Agent relationship
Intermediary relationship
No legal relationship exists
questions.explanation: Under W.S. §33-28-302(p), a customer relationship exists by default 'unless a single agency or intermediary relationship is established through a written agreement.' A customer is not a client, but Wyoming does not leave a customer with nothing: §33-28-310(a) requires reasonable skill and care, timely presentation of all offers, timely accounting, keeping the parties fully informed, and disclosure of adverse material facts actually known. What a customer is NOT owed is agency-level loyalty and fidelity — and §33-28-302(p) states flatly that a licensee 'shall not owe any duty of confidentiality to a customer.'

questions.question_text: An intermediary in Wyoming assists both buyer and seller. Which duty does the intermediary NOT owe?
distractors: Honesty in all dealings
Disclosure of material facts
Proper accounting of funds
questions.explanation: W.S. §33-28-305(a) provides that an intermediary 'shall not act as an advocate or agent for either party,' and §33-28-305(b)(ii)(K) requires the intermediary to disclose that an intermediary 'owes no fiduciary duty either to buyer or seller' and 'is not allowed to negotiate on behalf of the buyer or seller.' Loyalty and fidelity are agency duties under §§33-28-303(a)(iii) and 33-28-304(a)(iii) only. The intermediary still owes good faith and fair dealing (§33-28-302(g)), timely presentation of offers, timely accounting, and disclosure of adverse material facts (§33-28-305(b)(ii)(A), (C), (H), (J)).

questions.question_text: A licensee acting as an intermediary refuses to follow the seller's instruction to hide a foundation crack. Is this refusal proper?
questions.correct_answer: Yes, intermediaries must disclose material facts
distractors: No, intermediaries must obey all instructions
No, the seller's interests come first
Yes, but only if the buyer asks directly
questions.explanation: An intermediary is not an advocate or agent for either party (W.S. §33-28-305(a)) and must disclose adverse material facts actually known to prospective buyers and sellers alike (§33-28-305(b)(ii)(H), (J)). Concealing a known foundation defect would violate that disclosure duty and the good-faith-and-fair-dealing obligation of §33-28-302(g).

questions.question_text: A Wyoming licensee works with a buyer but has no written agency agreement. What relationship type exists?
distractors: Automatic buyer agency is created
An intermediary relationship by default
No relationship exists without a contract
questions.explanation: Under W.S. §33-28-302(p) a customer relationship exists by default; agency and intermediary relationships require a written agreement (§33-28-302(b) and (c)). Since 2026 (SF0105, eff. 7/1/2026) §33-28-102(b)(xiii) defines a 'customer' to include a person 'who attends a showing of real estate without any agency relationship.' A customer is still owed the §33-28-310(a) duties — reasonable skill and care, timely offer presentation, timely accounting, being kept fully informed, and disclosure of adverse material facts — but not loyalty or fidelity, and §33-28-302(p) says no duty of confidentiality is owed to a customer.

questions.question_text: A buyer's agent learns the seller is facing foreclosure. What must the agent do?
questions.correct_answer: Disclose this information to the buyer
distractors: Keep it confidential per fair dealing rules
Share it only if the seller consents
Report it to WREC before telling the buyer
questions.explanation: W.S. §33-28-304(a)(iii)(C) requires a buyer's agent to disclose to the buyer 'adverse material facts actually known by the licensee,' and (D) requires counseling the buyer on material benefits or risks actually known. A pending foreclosure is 'material to the transaction' under §33-28-102(b)(xxxii). The seller's protected-information list in §33-28-303(b) binds the seller's agent, not the buyer's agent, so nothing bars the disclosure.

questions.question_text: Which duty is owed to a customer but NOT elevated to fiduciary level?
distractors: Loyalty in all transactions
Obedience to lawful instructions
Confidentiality of negotiation strategy
questions.explanation: Good faith and fair dealing attach to every relationship in the article, including customer relationships (W.S. §33-28-302(g)). Loyalty and fidelity are reserved for agency (§§33-28-303(a)(iii), 33-28-304(a)(iii)); Wyoming's statute imposes no duty of 'obedience' at all; and confidentiality is expressly excluded — §33-28-302(p) states a licensee 'shall not owe any duty of confidentiality to a customer,' and §33-28-306(a)(vii)(B) requires that fact to be disclosed in writing. A customer is still owed the §33-28-310(a) duties of reasonable skill and care.

questions.question_text: An intermediary discovers termite damage during a showing. What is the intermediary's obligation?
questions.correct_answer: Disclose it to both buyer and seller
distractors: Disclose it only to the buyer
Keep it confidential until closing
Advise only the seller to get an inspection
questions.explanation: An intermediary must disclose material facts to both parties. Termite damage is an adverse material fact that affects property value. Unlike an agent who advocates for one side, the intermediary shares material information equally with both buyer and seller.

questions.question_text: A listing agent receives an offer but believes a higher one is coming tomorrow. The seller asks for advice. What should the agent do?
questions.correct_answer: Present the offer and share all known facts
distractors: Hold the offer until the better one arrives
Reject the offer on the seller's behalf
Present the offer but withhold the rumor
questions.explanation: W.S. §33-28-303(a)(iii)(B) requires a seller's agent 'to present all offers to and from the seller in a timely manner regardless of whether the property is subject to a contract for sale,' and (D) requires counseling the seller on material benefits or risks actually known. Combined with the reasonable-skill-and-care duty in §33-28-303(a)(ii), the agent must deliver the offer promptly and tell the seller what the agent knows about the possible second offer. (Wyoming's statute imposes no duty labeled 'obedience' — the duty is to perform the terms of the written agreement, §33-28-303(a)(i).)

questions.question_text: An intermediary keeps the buyer's maximum price confidential from the seller. Is this proper?
questions.correct_answer: Yes, certain confidential info is protected
distractors: No, all facts must be shared with both parties
No, the seller has a right to all buyer info
Yes, but only if the buyer requests it in writing
questions.explanation: An intermediary owes confidentiality of certain information, including a party's negotiation strategy or maximum price. While the intermediary must disclose material facts about the property, confidential bargaining information is protected for both sides.

questions.question_text: A Wyoming responsible broker's firm has one licensee working with the seller and a different licensee working with the buyer in the same in-house transaction. How does Wyoming law treat this?
questions.correct_answer: Simultaneous designated licensees — expressly not dual agency
distractors: Dual agency, permitted with both parties' written consent
An intermediary relationship the responsible broker must adopt
A prohibited arrangement — one party must move to another firm
questions.explanation: W.S. §33-28-302(j) allows licensees of the same responsible broker to 'be designated licensees for different buyers or sellers in the same transaction' and states that 'the simultaneous designations shall not constitute dual agency or require the responsible broker or licensee to act as an intermediary.' Each designated licensee may stay a full agent for their own party. Dual agency itself is banned outright by §33-28-302(o). The firm could instead convert to an intermediary relationship, but only with both parties' written consent under §33-28-307(a)(ii) — it is an option, not a requirement.

questions.question_text: How must a designated licensee be appointed in Wyoming?
questions.correct_answer: In writing by the responsible broker
distractors: Verbally at the first showing
By WREC upon application
Through mutual agreement of the parties
questions.explanation: W.S. §33-28-102(b)(xv) defines a 'designated licensee' as one 'designated in writing by a responsible broker to serve as an agent for a seller or a buyer or as an intermediary in a real estate transaction.' The designation must come from the responsible broker and must be in writing, and §33-28-302(k) requires the applicable designated relationship to be disclosed in writing to the seller and buyer at the earliest reasonable opportunity. Note the designation may be as an agent OR as an intermediary — an intermediary is expressly not an advocate (§33-28-305(a)).

questions.question_text: A Wyoming broker wants to represent both buyer and seller as a dual agent. Is this permitted?
questions.correct_answer: No, dual agency is prohibited in Wyoming
distractors: Yes, with written consent from both parties
Yes, if the broker discloses to WREC
Only for commercial transactions
questions.explanation: W.S. §33-28-302(o) states plainly: 'A licensee shall not establish dual agency with any seller or buyer.' §33-28-302(k) reinforces it — a licensee may act for the seller or for the buyer 'but not as an agent for both the seller and the buyer.' There is no written-consent exception. The lawful in-house alternatives are simultaneous designated licensees (§33-28-302(j), which 'shall not constitute dual agency or require the responsible broker or licensee to act as an intermediary'), or converting to an intermediary relationship with both parties' written consent under §33-28-307(a)(ii).

questions.question_text: Broker Smith designates Licensee A to work with the seller and Licensee B to work with the buyer in the same in-house transaction. Smith represents neither party. What is Smith's role?
questions.correct_answer: Supervising responsible broker, barred from sharing either party's confidential information
distractors: Dual agent for both parties
Intermediary for both parties by operation of law
Transaction coordinator owing no duties
questions.explanation: W.S. §33-28-302(j) provides that simultaneous designations 'shall not constitute dual agency or require the responsible broker or licensee to act as an intermediary,' so Smith does not become an intermediary. He stays the supervising responsible broker and 'shall have access to all necessary information but shall be prohibited from sharing any confidential information of any party.' Had Smith himself been representing a buyer or seller in the in-house transaction, §33-28-302(j) would require him to immediately appoint a transaction manager (unless the other licensee is an associate broker) — and under §33-28-102(b)(lx) that transaction manager 'shall have the duties of an intermediary while supervising the transaction.'

questions.question_text: Licensee A is the designated licensee for the buyer. A learns that the seller's designated licensee in the same firm revealed the seller's bottom-line price. What violation occurred?
questions.correct_answer: Breach of confidentiality by the seller's agent
distractors: No violation if the broker approved it
Breach of the intermediary's accounting duty
Violation of dual agency rules
questions.explanation: W.S. §33-28-303(b)(i) provides that a seller's agent shall not disclose, without the seller's informed consent, 'that a seller is willing to accept less than the asking price for the property.' Simultaneous designations within one firm are not dual agency and do not make anyone an intermediary (§33-28-302(j)), so each designated licensee keeps the full agent duties to their own party — including this protected-information restriction. The responsible broker could not have authorized the leak: §33-28-302(j) separately bars the responsible broker or transaction manager from sharing any party's confidential information.
